text: Time to apply CNOT, CZ, and the Bell-state recipe to specific problems and compute real answers, including a couple of results that aren't what intuition predicts until you actually do the arithmetic.

Apply CNOT with control q2, target q1 — the reverse of the usual direction — to the Bell state ket-00 plus ket-11 over root 2. You might guess this symmetric-looking state is unchanged. It isn't: the reversed gate flips the ket-11 term's first qubit, turning it into ket-01, while leaving ket-00 alone. The result is ket-00 plus ket-01 over root 2 — a completely different state. The symmetric look is deceptive, and running the actual matrix multiplication is what catches that.

Now take CZ, diagonal with a negative 1 only on ket-11, and apply it to that same original Bell state, ket-00 plus ket-11 over root 2. Only the ket-11 amplitude flips sign, giving ket-00 minus ket-11 over root 2. The measurement probabilities stay at 0.5 and 0.5 on ket-00 and ket-11 — CZ doesn't change what you'd measure here — but it moves you to a genuinely different member of the Bell-state family through a pure relative-phase flip.

The throughline across this lab: a symmetric-looking state is not automatically a fixed point of a symmetric-looking gate, different starting basis states need different gate sequences to reach the same target Bell state, and CZ can reassign which Bell state you're in without ever touching the measurement odds. In every case, the only reliable approach is the actual matrix-vector computation — never reasoning from how a state happens to look.
That closes out multi-qubit and entangling gates. Chapter 4 starts translating everything from these last two chapters into the circuit diagrams real quantum programming tools actually draw.
